Use this page to choose work that fits your interests and the equipment that is available. A mission may be assigned to the whole class, completed by a pair, or selected as an independent project.

**Not sure which mission to choose?** [Compare every mission by equipment, effort, circuits, coding, measurement, building, and troubleshooting.](mission-bank.qmd)

## Finish-strong pathway

1. Start with the [Breadboard and Raspberry Pi LED beginner mission](projects/beginner-breadboard-pi-led.qmd).
2. [Make your first Git checkpoint](projects/git-first-save.qmd).
3. [Open the Quarto starter and build your course website](projects/quarto-course-site.qmd).
4. Choose one achievable mission from the [Mission Bank](mission-bank.qmd).
5. Add the result to the website and make one more Git commit.

Git works locally without Wi-Fi. Public publishing is optional.

::: {.callout-important title="The rule for every powered load"}
A Raspberry Pi or BeagleBone sends a **control signal**. It does not power a pump, DC motor, relay coil, horn, automotive lamp, or LED strip. Those loads use a teacher-approved driver, protection, and separate supply.
:::

## Choose a mission

The labels tell you how the mission may be used:

- **Independent:** suitable for a student or pair working from the page.
- **Class:** suitable for a teacher-led transportation or computer-engineering lesson.
- **Teacher check:** the circuit must be inspected before power is connected.
- **Simulation first:** logic and calculations are tested before physical wiring.

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-lg-4}

## The same mission can serve two courses

| Route | Main evidence |
|:--|:--|
| Transportation class | Neat wiring, safe meter use, voltage-drop evidence, circuit operation, and fault diagnosis |
| Computer engineering | Schematic, calculations, simulation, Python, protected interface, measurements, and testing |
| Independent extension | A second input/output, data log, state machine, improved driver, or prepared troubleshooting challenge |

Students may work together on one physical system while submitting evidence for their own route.

## Standard mission sequence

1. Choose the minimum version.
2. Identify the exact parts and their ratings.
3. Draw or read the approved schematic.
4. Simulate the logic or circuit when a suitable simulator is available.
5. Calculate expected voltage, current, power, or timing.
6. Request the equipment.
7. Pass the power-off teacher check.
8. Build and test one stage at a time.
9. Measure the result and compare it with the prediction.
10. Demonstrate the system, submit the evidence, and return every issued part.

## Evidence required for every mission

- one readable schematic or approved wiring diagram;
- actual part numbers and ratings;
- calculations that match the circuit;
- expected and measured values with units;
- relevant code or simulation evidence;
- one problem, the evidence used to diagnose it, and the correction;
- clear photographs of the completed setup;
- a safe shutdown and complete equipment return.

## If the instructions are unclear

Name the exact heading or numbered step, state what you expected to happen, show what happened instead, and suggest one change that would make the page easier for the next group.
